text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

(Source - FinFloww on Whatsapp)

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

1. Supreme Court Orders Child Social Media Safeguards
A front-page report in Times of India says the Supreme Court has sought the government's response to a public interest litigation arguing that opening social media accounts equates to entering into a legal contract, which is legally impermissible for individuals under eighteen years of age. The court emphasised the urgent need for digital safeguards and firewalls to shield children from online grooming, cyberbullying, and data exploitation. Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.
Despite being aware of this menace for years, successive governments have failed to implement a robust national mechanism to identify and deport such individuals.

8. The Hope:- Now that the Home Minister himself has spoken openly about the issue, one can only hope it translates into real, concrete action. India needs a firm, technology-backed, corruption-proof mechanism to detect and remove non-Indians living here on forged documents.

Illegal infiltration is not just a demographic concern, it’s a threat to national integrity, law, and fairness. The time for acknowledgment is over.
The time for action has arrived.

Subject: Request for Investigation - Andhra Pradesh Police Officer Identified “FBI” as Requesting Organization in X/Twitter Law-Enforcement Request Concerning a U.S. Citizen

To:
Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
@FBI @FBIDirectorKash @FBITampa @TheJusticeDept  
U.S. Department of Justice

Dear Director / Appropriate Federal Officials:

I am a United States citizen residing in the United States. I respectfully submit this complaint and request for review concerning an apparent misrepresentation of U.S. federal law-enforcement identity in connection with a social-media investigation initiated by the Andhra Pradesh Police in India.

I. Summary of the complaint

I recently received a notification from X Support concerning a law-enforcement request submitted to X regarding my X account.
The X communication initially stated that the request had been submitted by the “FBI.”

However, X subsequently provided an important correction. X expressly stated:

“However, this request did not come from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)”

X further stated that the request actually came from the Andhra Pradesh Police and identified the submitting individual as:

Name: A V Bramham
Position: Inspector of Police
Organization entered by requester: FBI
Email: guntururbansp-ap@gov.in
Location: Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India
Country: India

X further stated:
“it is unclear why the Andhra Pradesh Police wrote ‘FBI’ as the sender organization.”
I have preserved the X communication and can provide the original notification and screenshot as evidence.
II. Why I am requesting U.S. government review
I fully recognize that foreign law-enforcement agencies may communicate with U.S. companies through legitimate international law-enforcement cooperation channels.
The issue here is different.

According to X’s own records, an Andhra Pradesh Police official submitted the request, but the requesting organization was entered as “FBI.”

I therefore respectfully request that the appropriate U.S. authorities determine:

Whether the FBI had any involvement whatsoever in this request to X.

Whether any FBI office, agent, liaison officer, or other U.S. government agency authorized, participated in, or communicated with Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my X account.
Whether the Andhra Pradesh Police official knowingly or inadvertently represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting the request to X.

Whether the use of “FBI” as the requesting organization was intended to obtain greater credibility, priority, cooperation, disclosure, restriction, or removal of content from X.

Whether X received any other law-enforcement request from Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account in which the FBI was similarly identified.

Whether this conduct implicates any U.S. federal criminal, civil-rights, cyber, impersonation, transnational-repression, or other federal jurisdiction.

Whether the conduct should be referred to another appropriate federal authority for investigation.
III. First Amendment / transnational-repression concern
The underlying matter concerns social-media content posted on X and alleged violations of Indian law.
I am particularly concerned because I am a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, and the governmental action concerns my online speech and political commentary.
I understand that the United States cannot simply disregard legitimate foreign criminal investigations. However, I am requesting that U.S. authorities determine whether a foreign law-enforcement agency has attempted to use the identity or authority of a U.S. federal agency to influence or restrict constitutionally protected activity occurring in the United States.
The FBI itself recognizes transnational repression as an issue that may affect people in the United States and specifically directs individuals who believe they have been affected by transnational repression to report the matter to the FBI.
IV. Request for preservation and investigation of evidence
I respectfully request that the appropriate agency consider preserving and/or obtaining, where legally appropriate:
the original law-enforcement request submitted by Andhra Pradesh Police to X;

all metadata associated with that request;

the identity and authentication information associated with the requester;

the date and time of submission;

all representations made by the requester concerning his identity and governmental organization;
any attachments, legal documents, FIRs, court orders, or other materials submitted to X;

any subsequent communications between X and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account;
any communications between U.S. government agencies and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning this matter; and
any evidence showing whether “FBI” was entered intentionally or accidentally.
V. Request for clarification from the FBI
I respectfully request confirmation of the following:
Did the FBI have any involvement in, authorization of, or knowledge of this particular request to X?
If the answer is no, I respectfully request that the FBI consider whether the circumstances warrant investigation or referral concerning the apparent use of the FBI’s identity by a foreign law-enforcement official.
VI. Good-faith submission
I am not asking the U.S. government to interfere with a legitimate Indian criminal investigation.
My request is narrower:
I am asking the United States government to determine whether an Indian police official represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting a law-enforcement request concerning a U.S. citizen’s social-media account, and whether that conduct violated any U.S. law or raised a transnational-repression or foreign-government intimidation concern.

I am prepared to provide the original X communication, screenshots, account information, relevant posts, and any notices received from Andhra Pradesh Police.

I respectfully request that this complaint be logged, reviewed, and referred to the appropriate federal authority if the receiving office does not have jurisdiction.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Respectfully,

U.S. Citizen

text:
13 Defining Legal & Regulatory Stories for Compliance Officers
https://t.co/8yLw5p4pdP

Today's legal & regulatory landscape shifts fast. Welcome to your essential press review tracking India's top judicial rulings and enforcement actions. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, our media intelligence engine filters thousands of pages to deliver actionable insights, proving why print media monitoring remains the gold standard for verified business data. Below, we break down the most impactful proceedings shaping compliance, litigation strategy, and corporate governance.

1. Delhi High Court Mandates Biometric GST Verification
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Delhi High Court has ordered all Goods and Services Tax authorities across the nation to mandate biometric Aadhaar authentication alongside PAN verification before issuing new registrations. Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain passed this directive on 8 September to halt rampant identity fraud, with arguments resuming on 22 September.
Why it matters: Streamlines tax compliance and curbs identity fraud.
Key detail: Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain ordered mandatory Aadhaar authentication alongside PAN checks for new registrations, halting rampant misuse.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Tax authorities must implement biometric protocols immediately; stakeholders should monitor updated GST portal guidelines.

2. Bombay High Court Acquits Convict Due to Evidentiary Gaps
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Bombay High Court has acquitted Debashish Dhara, ruling that insufficient evidence linked him to the rape and murder of a twenty-four-year-old physiotherapist in Vile Parle on December sixth two thousand sixteen. The judges emphasised that suspicion cannot replace proof and that doubtful circumstances cannot accumulate to create certainty of guilt. The court accordingly set aside his conviction and death sentence.
Why it matters: Reinforces the presumption of innocence and evidentiary standards in criminal trials.
Key detail: Judges ruled that suspicion cannot replace proof, setting aside a death sentence due to insufficient evidence linking Debashish Dhara to the crime.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Defense teams should cite this precedent when challenging convictions reliant on circumstantial evidence.

3. Supreme Court Intervenes in Minor Intimidation Allegations
A front-page report in Statesman says the Supreme Court has taken serious note of allegations made on Thursday, September tenth, regarding a fourteen-year-old girl associated with the protests being intimidated and having stones pelted at her residence. The bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, emphasised that threats to minors cannot be overlooked and warned against intimidating victims involved in criminal proceedings. The court maintained that permitting anti-social individuals to target children undermines justice and demands strict enforcement.
Why it matters: Protects vulnerable witnesses and upholds judicial integrity amid public agitation.
Key detail: Chief Justice Surya Kant's bench warned against intimidating minors involved in proceedings, directing immediate security assessments.
Source: Statesman
Next step: Local police must submit compliance reports; legal advocates should track the committee's findings.

4. Supreme Court Orders Immediate Protection for NEET Student
A front-page report in The Hindu says the Supreme Court asked Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta to ensure immediate action on a complaint filed by a fourteen-year-old student who alleged open threats and harassment from miscreants for her role in protests against NEET-UG question paper leaks. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, heading a three-judge Bench, observed that anti-social elements commit violence against a child and roam free, and urged Uttar Pradesh Police to take responsibility for the safety of the student and her family. The student's counsel argued that vulnerable victims should be able to safeguard their privacy by directly approaching the top court or accessing the Supreme Court-appointed High-Powered Enquiry Committee.
Why it matters: Safeguards student activists facing harassment over academic integrity protests.
Key detail: CJI Surya Kant directed Uttar Pradesh Police to secure the fourteen-year-old's safety, emphasizing state responsibility for vulnerable complainants.
Source: The Hindu
Next step: Students and parents should utilize the Supreme Court-appointed High-Powered Enquiry Committee for grievance redressal.

5. Delhi Court Frames PMLA Charges Against Lalu Prasad Family
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says a Delhi court ordered framing of money laundering charges against Rashtriya Janata Dal president Lalu Prasad Yadav, his wife Rabri Devi, son Tejashwi Yadav and six others in a case linked to alleged irregularities in the leasing of two Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation hotels when Lalu Prasad was the railway minister. Special Judge Vishal Gogne said there was strong suspicion that abuse of office by Lalu Prasad generated proceeds of crime that came into the hands of Rabri Devi and Tejashwi Yadav, who continue to enjoy the use of the allegedly tainted land in Patna. The court said prima facie the tender process for railway hotels in Ranchi and Puri was manipulated during Lalu Prasad tenure as railway minister, with contracts awarded to Sujata Hotels Pvt Ltd in an alleged quid pro quo arrangement, and formal charges will be framed on October 3.
Why it matters: Signals heightened enforcement scrutiny over public sector tender manipulation.
Key detail: Special Judge Vishal Gogne found sufficient material under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act regarding IRCTC hotel leases, charging nine accused including former railway minister Lalu Prasad, Rabri Devi, and Tejashwi Yadav.
Source: Hindustan Times
Next step: Corporate governance officers must audit historical tender processes; political watchers should follow the October 3 charge formalization.

6. Supreme Court Retains Jurisdiction Over Delhi PG Collapse Inquiry
A front-page report in Morning Standard says the Supreme Court declined to transfer the Satya Niketan building collapse case to its own bench, directing the High Court to continue monitoring as enforcement actions progress. Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R Mahadevan heard the suo motu matter concerning nationwide building bye-law violations, while Solicitor General Tushar Mehta confirmed that municipal authorities have begun demolishing structures exceeding four storeys. The court noted ongoing inspections across Delhi and Lucknow and will review compliance reports on 15 September.
Why it matters: Ensures consistent oversight of urban infrastructure violations and building code compliance.
Key detail: The apex court declined to transfer the Satya Niketan case, directing the Delhi High Court to monitor demolitions and municipal suspensions while nationwide bye-law inspections continue.
Source: Morning Standard
Next step: Real estate developers and municipal bodies must align with upgraded structural safety audits ahead of the September 15 compliance review.

7. Supreme Court Rejects Reconstitution of Protest Inquiry Committee
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Supreme Court on Thursday ruled out changes to the five-member high-powered committee headed by former Supreme Court judge R Subhash Reddy, constituted to examine allegations of police excesses against student protesters in Delhi and violence against police personnel. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it would not presume that a committee constituted by the court was biased. Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for a petitioner seeking reconstitution, said a former Meghalaya Director General of Police on the panel faced a conflict of interest because of his alleged proximity to a functionary likely to come under investigation.
Why it matters: Maintains institutional credibility and procedural continuity in high-stakes investigations.
Key detail: A three-judge bench refused petitioner demands to alter the five-member panel, stating courts do not presume bias in their own constituted committees.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Stakeholders should engage with the existing committee's helpline mechanism for witness submissions.

8. Supreme Court Questions Legal Authority Behind Delhi Metro Shutdowns
A front-page report in Times of India says special judge Vishal Gogne of the Rouse Avenue Court has framed charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad, his wife Rabri Devi, son Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, and six others for money laundering linked to an Irctc hotel scam. The allegations trace back to Lalu's tenure during the Upa government from 2004 to 2009, with the court observing that tender manipulation occurred under his stewardship. Former Rjd union minister Premchand Gupta, his wife Sarla, and Lara Projects were also named among those charged.
Why it matters: Clarifies jurisdictional boundaries between police directives and public transport operations during civil unrest.
Key detail: Justice Joymalya Bagchi highlighted that vehicle movement regulation falls under police authority, not metro corporations, prompting responses from the central government and DMRC.
Source: Times of India
Next step: Transport administrators should review emergency closure protocols against the Metro Railways Act.

9. Supreme Court Upholds Mumbai University Law College Intake Reduction
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Supreme Court on Thursday declined to interfere with the Bombay High Court's dismissal of a PIL challenging Mumbai University's decision to halve the sanctioned intake at several affiliated law colleges. The three-judge bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant upheld the Bombay High Court order, which had rejected the plea filed by the Lawyers' Foundation, but set aside the cost of 1 lakh rupees imposed on the petitioner. The university had decided to reduce intake by fifty percent in three-year and five-year LLB programmes at around forty-five affiliated colleges for the 2026-27 academic year after identifying deficiencies including inadequate faculty.
Why it matters: Prioritizes educational quality over institutional expansion in professional courses.
Key detail: The bench upheld the Bombay High Court's dismissal of a PIL challenging fifty percent intake cuts at forty-five affiliated colleges due to faculty deficiencies.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Law schools must accelerate faculty recruitment and infrastructure upgrades to meet UGC benchmarks.

10. Supreme Court Suspends Noida Magistrate for Coercive Protest Notices
A front-page report in The Hindu says Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta informed the Supreme Court on Thursday about the suspension of an Executive Magistrate of the Greater Noida Commissionerate. The Magistrate issued a show-cause notice to a student in connection with the recent protests at Jantar Mantar despite a Supreme Court order prohibiting coercive measures against students part of the agitation.
Why it matters: Reinforces judicial orders protecting peaceful assembly and student rights.
Key detail: Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta confirmed the suspension of an executive magistrate who issued show-cause notices despite explicit court prohibitions on coercive measures.
Source: The Hindu
Next step: Administrative officers must cross-reference ongoing injunctions before issuing compliance directives.

11. High Court Reinstates Judicial Officer’s Performance Appraisal
A front-page report in First India says that the High Court’s administrative wing reversed a May two thousand twenty six judgment that had removed adverse remarks from Goyal’s APAR two thousand. The court found no evidence of misconduct, noting the entries for the two periods were made with the same ink and handwriting, suggesting record manipulation, and directed that Goyal’s APAR be treated as good and his integrity not regarded as doubtful, extending benefits. Senior advocate Virendra Lodha appeared for Raj HC, referring to Goyal’s record, including an allegation that he had applied for a petrol pump as a judicial officer.
Why it matters: Guards against record manipulation and protects career progression in public service.
Key detail: The administrative wing reversed a prior judgment removing adverse remarks, noting identical ink and handwriting patterns indicated forged entries, restoring full benefits.
Source: First India
Next step: Civil servants should document appraisal discrepancies early and seek judicial review when records show tampering.

12. Supreme Court Clarifies Boundaries of High-Powered Probe Committees
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says the Supreme Court of India clarified on Thursday that its five-member high-powered enquiry committee cannot order registration of FIRs regarding the July protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party, stating that the power to direct criminal investigations rests exclusively with the court. The bench emphasised that the committee must work under the direct supervision of the court and permitted it to give wide publicity to its proceedings, invite suggestions, and create a dedicated mechanism including a helpline for vulnerable witnesses.
Why it matters: Defines operational limits of quasi-judicial bodies to prevent overreach into criminal investigation mandates.
Key detail: The bench emphasized that FIR registration power rests exclusively with courts, permitting the committee to publicize proceedings and establish witness protection mechanisms instead.
Source: Hindustan Times
Next step: Legal practitioners should leverage the committee's helpline for sensitive testimony while respecting investigative jurisdiction.

13. International Judicial Ethics Spotlight: US Judge Reprimanded
A front-page report in Deccan Chronicle says the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court issued a public reprimand against Judge Shelley Joseph on Thursday, following accusations that she colluded with an immigrant’s attorney and a court officer to allow an illegal immigrant to escape from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody through a courthouse back door in Boston. The case dates back to 2018, and the court rejected claims of innocence presented by Joseph’s attorney Elizabeth Mulvey that the case had been distorted. The ruling cited the judge’s actions as creating an appearance of impropriety and violating her duties under the law.
Why it matters: Highlights global standards for judicial conduct and immigration custody protocols.
Key detail: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court publicly reprimanded Judge Shelley Joseph for facilitating an escape from ICE custody, citing appearances of impropriety and duty violations.
Source: Deccan Chronicle
Next step: Judicial training institutes worldwide are reviewing custody handover procedures following this ruling.

Meta has agreed to report cases involving child sexual abuse to law enforcement agencies, amid the Centre’s efforts to strengthen child safety across social media platforms.

Officials stressed that ensuring children’s online safety is a fundamental responsibility of platforms operating in India. They also warned that action could be taken against platforms that fail to adopt proactive measures to protect children.

The development comes after the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta India representatives on September 9 over allegations involving advertisements linked to child sexual exploitation and abuse material on Meta-owned platforms.

The NCPCR launched a probe after taking note of a BBC Eye report on alleged advertisements promoting such material. Meta had submitted its response a week after receiving the commission’s notice in July.

Meanwhile, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has directed Delhi Police to conduct a comprehensive investigation into allegations that paid Instagram advertisements promoted child sexual exploitation and abuse material in India. Police have also been asked to examine Meta and other platforms’ compliance with mandatory reporting requirements under the POCSO Act.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). text:
Can we talk about Meta's glasses for a second?

They look like ordinary sunglasses, and the only warning is a tiny LED most people never notice. In just three weeks, we've sent two legal notices to Meta. One is for a man secretly filmed and mocked at a Delhi café. The other is for a woman covertly recorded on her walk home for a "pickup artist's" Instagram content.

Being in public shouldn't mean becoming someone's content without your consent. This is NOT normal.

Here are the two legal notices we sent to Meta over its Ray-Ban smart glasses:

Case 1: Harassment for clout
A man sitting alone at a café was harassed and secretly filmed, and the video was posted to mock him. We're seeking ₹2.05 crore in damages.
Read more: https://t.co/l8nJZDlX3w

Case 2: Stalking as "pickup" content
A woman walking home was covertly recorded to sell "approach classes" on Instagram. She filed a police complaint, and we sent Meta a second notice.
Read more: https://t.co/GXoD9IHFZd

If you've ever been filmed like this without your consent, you're not alone, and it's not okay. Please share this with someone who should know.

We do this work with support from people like you: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

Phone jammers 👇🏽👇🏽

quotedTweet.text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

On 8 September, IFF filed three RTIs with the Delhi Police. We are seeking records on every jammer it possesses, the permissions and procurement documents, the officers authorised to deploy them, the applicable SOPs and deployment registers, and the specific records concerning Jantar Mantar on 20 and 22 July. We have also asked for the records behind the Satya Niketan denial. (9/10)

The question is not whether telecommunications can ever be restricted. Indian law already provides a framework for temporary suspension of services. The question is whether a separate, less visible mechanism can bypass those safeguards and cut communications without the written order, publication, review and accountability that accompany a lawful shutdown. IFF will publish the Delhi Police's replies, including any silence, and continue seeking clarity on who can jam communications, for what purpose and under what law. (10/10)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

The concern is not hypothetical. Meta announced in July that a firmware update would disable the camera when the recording light is tampered with. Around the same period, Instagram said it would remove harassment videos filmed using Meta glasses, specifically identifying “pickup line” videos. Yet this reel, filmed as pickup content using the glasses, remained online for weeks after those announcements. (8/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)
